tagline: North through a wildlife corridor to a ferry town and border crossing.
intro: Sandpoint stands on Lake Pend Oreille, surrounded by the Selkirk, Cabinet and Bitterroot mountain ranges. North of town, US 95 crosses the McArthur Lake Wildlife Corridor on its way to Bonners Ferry. Conifer forests, wetlands, streams and rivers form the corridor’s landscape. Farther north, State Highway 1 connects US 95 east of Copeland with Porthill on the Canadian boundary. US 95 bypasses downtown Sandpoint on a divided highway along the waterfront; at McArthur Lake, the road runs beside the reservoir’s east shore.

The historic Wildhorse Trail carried thousands of prospectors north after gold was discovered in British Columbia’s East Kootenays in 1863. The following year, Walla Walla merchant Edwin Bonner established a ferry where that trail crossed the Kootenai River. The numbered highway came later: State Highway 1 developed from the 1920s Sampson Trail B and entered Idaho’s new numbering system in the mid-1930s.

Travel north from Sandpoint on US 95, passing the east shore of McArthur Lake before Bonners Ferry. Beyond Bonners Ferry, State Highway 1 branches from US 95 east of Copeland and leads to Porthill. At the border, it meets British Columbia Highway 21; the north-flowing Kootenai River lies just west of Porthill.

moments.title: McArthur Lake Wildlife Corridor
moments.text: The highway crosses a route used by grizzly bears moving between the Selkirk and Cabinet mountains. Deer and other hoofed animals also winter here. A highway, two railway lines, buildings and fences share the corridor with that movement. The highway has high rates of wildlife collisions, and difficult terrain limits options for safe crossings. Conservation groups have obtained easements on timberland to restrict further development while allowing sustainable forestry. In September 2016, about 5,568 acres of forest east of McArthur Lake received conservation easements limiting development and subdivision while retaining forestry.

moments.title: Bonners Ferry
moments.text: Brick buildings on Main Street belong to a town that once perched on stilts against spring floods. Bonners Ferry grew at the Kootenai River crossing established by Edwin Bonner in 1864. Richard Fry and his Sinixt wife, Justine Su-steel Fry, leased the ferry business in 1875, but Bonner’s name remained. As the town became a lumbering and farming center, valley land was drained and levees were built. Much of Main Street dates from the period when brick replaced the stilt-supported buildings. Completion of Libby Dam in 1975 reduced the threat of serious flooding, another change in the town’s relationship with the river.

moments.title: Porthill
moments.text: The border settlement was once called Ockonook, meaning “a grassy hillside with rocks.” Charles Plummer Hill took over as its US customs officer in 1893. As postmaster in 1897, he succeeded in renaming the settlement Porthill. The border buildings changed too: in 1967, the United States replaced its 1938 brick station with a wooden structure in a different location. The earlier building was preserved and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2014. The north-flowing Kootenai River lies west of town; at the crossing, Idaho Highway 1 joins British Columbia Highway 21 toward Creston.
